Genesis Chapter 1

Tap any verse below and its context and meaning will open right there

How to use: Each verse shows its text first. Tap it to reveal the context and the explanation. Inside the explanation, every scripture reference is tappable and opens that exact passage in the NKJV on Bible Gateway. The verse text is the King James Version (free to share); tap "Read in NKJV" to see the same verse in the New King James translation.

Book: Genesis (Hebrew: Bereshit, "In the beginning")

Theme of Genesis 1: The account of creation — God speaking the universe into existence in six days.

Chapter Overview

Genesis means "origin" or "beginning." Moses is the traditional author, writing for a people (Israel) recently delivered from Egypt, who needed to know who the true God was and why the world existed. Genesis 1 answers the great questions every human asks: Where did everything come from? Who am I? Why am I here?

  • Days 1–3: God forms the spaces (light/dark, sky/sea, land).
  • Days 4–6: God fills those spaces with inhabitants (lights, birds/fish, animals/humans).
  • Day 7 (Genesis 2:1–3): God rests.

The God of Israel is shown as supreme over everything the pagan nations worshipped — sun, moon, sea, and creatures are not gods; they are His handiwork.

GENESIS 1:1 "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: This is the opening line of the entire Bible. There is no argument for God's existence here — the Bible never debates whether God exists; it simply declares that He does and that everything begins with Him.

Meaning: The Hebrew word for "created" is bara — a word used only of God in the Bible, meaning to create something out of nothing. Humans can make things, but only out of materials that already exist. God alone creates from nothing. "The heaven and the earth" is a way of saying "everything" — the whole universe, visible and invisible. This verse establishes two non-negotiable truths: the universe had a beginning, and God was there before that beginning. Everything you will ever read in Scripture flows from this: if God made everything, then everything belongs to Him, answers to Him, and exists for His purpose. Before you understand yourself, your problems, or your future, you must understand that life begins with God.

GENESIS 1:2 "And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Between verse 1 and verse 2 we have a planet that exists but is unformed and uninhabited. The Hebrew phrase is tohu wa-bohu — "formless and empty," a scene of chaos, darkness, and water covering everything.

Meaning: Before God brings order, the earth is dark, shapeless, and empty. This is a picture God repeats in human lives: He often starts with darkness and emptiness, then brings form, order, and fullness. Notice that even in the chaos, God is present — "the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." The Hebrew suggests a hovering, a brooding, like a bird watching over its nest. God is never absent from the dark places; He is hovering over them, about to speak. Whatever is formless and empty in your life is raw material for the Spirit of God, not evidence of His absence.

GENESIS 1:3 "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The first act of creation recorded in detail. Notice the method: God speaks. No struggle, no ingredients, no process — a word.

Meaning: Light appears before the sun (which is created on day four), so this light is not natural sunlight; it is God's own radiance breaking into darkness. Throughout Scripture, light represents God's presence, truth, and life — and darkness represents death, sin, and separation from God. The first thing God commands into existence is light, because God's nature is light (1 John 1:5). The New Testament tells us that this same God who said "Let there be light" is the One who "hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6). When God begins a work, He begins by turning on the light.

GENESIS 1:4 "And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: This is the first time God evaluates His creation — "it was good." This phrase will repeat at the end of nearly every creative act.

Meaning: Two things stand out. First, God inspects His own work and pronounces it good — creation is not evil or flawed at its origin; evil enters later through sin (chapter 3). When God makes something, it is good by design. Second, God separates: He divides light from darkness. God is a God of order, not confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33), and throughout the Bible He consistently separates — holy from unholy, Israel from the nations, sheep from goats. From the very first day, God establishes the principle that light and darkness are not meant to mix. This is why believers are called to live separated, distinct lives — children of the light (Ephesians 5:8).

GENESIS 1:5 "And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: In the ancient world, naming something was an act of authority. Kings named cities to show dominion over them.

Meaning: God names the light "Day" and the darkness "Night" — He exercises authority over both. Night does not frighten God; He made it, named it, and set its boundary. Then the verse gives the Bible's way of measuring a day: "the evening and the morning." The Hebrew day begins at sunset, which is why the Jewish Sabbath begins at sundown. Notice the order — evening before morning. In God's economy, the night comes before the dawn. The believer's experience follows this pattern: weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning (Psalm 30:5). Whatever day of life you are in, God has numbered it, named it, and bounded it.

GENESIS 1:6 "And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Day two. The earth is still covered in water, and God now creates a "firmament" — the Hebrew raqia, meaning an expanse, a spread-out space.

Meaning: The firmament is the atmosphere and sky — the space between the waters on the earth (seas) and the waters above (clouds and the vapour canopy). God is building a home for life: without an atmosphere there is no air to breathe, no sky for birds, no water cycle for rain. Here is the remarkable truth: before God creates any creature, He first prepares the environment that creature will need. God never births life into a place He has not first prepared. This is a father's heart — He makes a home before He makes a family. The same God who prepared the sky before the birds will prepare the path before your steps (Psalm 37:23).

GENESIS 1:7 "And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament: and it was so." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The command of verse 6 is now performed. Notice the pattern forming throughout this chapter: God says it, God makes it, "and it was so."

Meaning: What God says, God does. There is no gap between God's word and God's work — His Word never returns to Him void (Isaiah 55:11). The "waters under" and "waters above" describe a designed water system: oceans below, moisture and clouds above, held in perfect balance. Scientists still marvel that earth alone in our solar system has liquid water in the exact quantities for life — the Bible described this design thousands of years before science confirmed it. When your life feels like it is divided and separated in ways you don't understand, remember: God's dividing is always for order and protection, not chaos. He separated the waters so life could flourish between them.

GENESIS 1:8 "And God called the firmament Heaven. And the evening and the morning were the second day." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: God names the expanse "Heaven" (shamayim in Hebrew). Interestingly, day two is the only day without the phrase "and God saw that it was good" — possibly because the heavens are the domain where spiritual conflict will later unfold (Ephesians 6:12, Daniel 10).

Meaning: The heaven named here is the physical sky, the space where clouds move and birds fly — not the dwelling place of God's glory (that is called the "heaven of heavens," 1 Kings 8:27). God is so vast that the highest heaven cannot contain Him, yet He chooses to be involved in the smallest details of this small planet. The same sky that seems empty to the natural eye is full of God's activity — His storehouses of rain, His highway for answered prayers, the stage where His signs will appear (Joel 2:30–31). Look up today: the sky is not an accident; it is architecture.

GENESIS 1:9 "And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Day three begins. The water covering the whole planet is commanded to gather into "one place" — the ocean basins — so that dry land can emerge.

Meaning: God sets boundaries for the sea. Scripture celebrates this repeatedly: "He hath commanded the sea, saying, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further" (Job 38:11; Jeremiah 5:22). The sea obeys God. This reveals a powerful principle: in God's kingdom, gathering comes before appearing. The waters gathered first, and then the land appeared. Before anything is revealed in your life, God first gathers — He gathers your scattered thoughts, your scattered resources, your scattered years — and then the dry ground appears on which He will build something. The disciples had to gather in the upper room before the Spirit appeared (Acts 2:1–4).

GENESIS 1:10 "And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The naming continues — Earth and Seas. God names the dry land and the waters, again demonstrating total ownership and authority over the planet.

Meaning: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein" (Psalm 24:1). Because God made the land and the sea, no person, government, or spirit ultimately owns the ground you stand on — God does. This is why the believer can stand with confidence: your footing belongs to your Father. Also notice: God looks at gathered waters and dry ground and calls it good. Land that appears out of water is a picture of resurrection — what was buried under the flood emerges to bear life. On the third day, the ground appears; and on another third day, the ground opened and the risen Christ appeared. God loves third days.

GENESIS 1:11 "And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Now that dry land exists, God fills it with vegetation. Three categories: grass, seed-bearing herbs, and fruit trees. Each carries its own seed "in itself."

Meaning: Two great truths here. First, life carries the power of continuation — the seed is in itself. God built reproduction into creation; every living thing carries within it the ability to produce the next generation. When God creates, He creates things that keep giving. Second, "after his kind" — a phrase repeated ten times in this chapter. Apple seeds produce apple trees; dogs produce dogs. This is God's established order, and it extends spiritually: whatever you sow, that is what reproduces (Galatians 6:7). If you want a harvest of blessing, you must sow the seed of blessing. God designed a world where seed is destiny — and He placed the seed of His Word in you so His life would reproduce in you.

GENESIS 1:12 "And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The earth obeys God's command and produces exactly what was commanded — no mutations, no half-formed plants, everything "after his kind."

Meaning: The earth heard God and responded. Jesus would later say the rocks could cry out if His disciples kept silent (Luke 19:40) — creation itself knows its Maker's voice. Notice also the fruit tree yielding fruit "whose seed is in itself" — inside every fruit is the seed of the next harvest. Ministry works this way: the fruit of a believer's life (a transformed soul, a healed family) contains the seed of someone else's salvation. God's design is never just for one generation. Every good thing God does through you is engineered to outlive you, if you let the seed fall into the ground rather than keeping the fruit to yourself (John 12:24).

GENESIS 1:13 "And the evening and the morning were the third day." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The close of day three. In three days God has formed light, sky, seas, dry land, and vegetation — the stage is nearly set for living creatures.

Meaning: The third day is the first day called "good" twice (verse 10 and verse 12) — the day life first appears on the earth. Grass, herbs, and trees are the first visible, living things God makes, and they come before any creature is made to enjoy them. God's provision always precedes His population: the food was ready before the eater existed. This is the heart of your Father — "your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things" (Matthew 6:32). He plants the garden before He forms the child. Before God asks you to occupy any place, He has already stocked it.

GENESIS 1:14 "And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years:" ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Day four. God now fills the light-bearing role with physical bodies: sun, moon, and stars. The light of day one is now entrusted to created objects.

Meaning: The heavenly lights are given four jobs: to divide, to signal ("signs"), and to mark "seasons, days, and years." Scripture says the heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1) — the sky is God's billboard. The star that led the wise men to Christ (Matthew 2:2) and the sun that stood still for Joshua (Joshua 10:13) both show creation serving God's redemptive story. Most importantly, God assigns seasons. Your life has seasons too — "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecclesiastes 3:1). The God who ordered the heavens has ordered your times. When your season feels dark, remember: the same sky that holds the night holds the instruments of dawn.

GENESIS 1:15 "And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The purpose of the sun, moon, and stars is defined: to give light upon the earth. They were not made for themselves; they were made to serve.

Meaning: Everything God creates is created to serve something else. The sun exists to give light; it was not created to enjoy its own brightness. This is the law of created purpose: nothing in God's design exists for itself alone. Jesus embodied this principle: "the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister" (Mark 10:45). You were created to be light for others — "Ye are the light of the world" (Matthew 5:14). The moon has no light of its own; it reflects the sun. That is the believer's identity: we have no light of our own, but we can reflect the Sun of Righteousness (Malachi 4:2) so that the world has light in its night.

GENESIS 1:16 "And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The sun is called the "greater light" and the moon the "lesser light," and both are given a rulership — over day and night respectively. Then, almost as an afterthought: "he made the stars also."

Meaning: Notice what God does NOT say. He does not name the sun and moon by the names used by the pagan nations (like Shamash the sun-god), because the nations worshipped these objects. God calls them simply lights — created objects with jobs, not deities with power. This was a direct confrontation with idolatry: don't worship the things God made; worship the God who made the things. And the throwaway line "he made the stars also" — with a breath God scattered one hundred billion galaxies. The immensity of the universe exists as a casual footnote to Genesis. How great is the God you serve? If He made the stars as a side note, no problem in your life is beyond His main sentence.

GENESIS 1:17 "And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth," ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: God does not just make the lights; He sets them — He positions them with intention.

Meaning: Placement matters. The sun is exactly the right distance from the earth — a little closer and we would burn, a little further and we would freeze. Scientists call this the "habitable zone"; Genesis simply says God set them there. God's placement is always purposeful: "He hath made every thing beautiful in his time" (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Where God has set you — your family, your church, your workplace, your nation — is not random. Esther was set in the palace "for such a time as this" (Esther 4:14). Before you resent your position, ask what God intends to illuminate through it. The lights were set in heaven for the sake of the earth below — you are set in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6) for the sake of people around you.

GENESIS 1:18 "And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The sun and moon are given authority — "to rule" — over day and night, and again God divides light from darkness.

Meaning: Rulership in God's kingdom means service, not domination: the sun rules the day by giving itself. True authority gives light, warmth, and life to those beneath it. This is why Jesus washed feet before He commanded disciples — "whosoever will be great among you, let him be your servant" (Matthew 20:26). If God has given you any position of influence, remember the model of the lights: rule by shining, not by scorching. And once more, God divides light from darkness — the fourth time separation appears in this chapter. God is holy, and He builds walls of distinction. The church loses its power when it blends with the night; it gains the world when it shines against it.

GENESIS 1:19 "And the evening and the morning were the fourth day." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Day four closes with the heavenly order established: light divided, times appointed, rulers set.

Meaning: By the end of day four, creation is ready to host life, because a world needs time to live in. God created the calendar before He created the creatures. This teaches us that God is a God of time — He works by appointment. "Hath he said, and shall he not do it?" (Numbers 23:19). The Psalmist says the days of the wicked are numbered; the days of the godly are ordered (Psalm 37:18). The evening-then-morning rhythm again whispers the gospel pattern: night first, then day. If you are in your evening — your dark season — hold on; God has built mornings into the fabric of creation.

GENESIS 1:20 "And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Day five. The first creatures with nephesh — living souls, breathing creatures — come from the waters and the sky.

Meaning: "Bring forth abundantly" — God is extravagant. A single drop of ocean water teems with life He spoke into being on this day. Science still cannot count the species of the sea; every expedition finds more. Notice that the water that once covered the earth in chaos (verse 2) is now commanded to become the nursery of life. God specializes in turning dark, deep places into sources of abundance. The tears and depths of your past are exactly where God loves to birth life. He does not merely remove the waters of chaos — He makes them fruitful (Psalm 46:4: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God").

GENESIS 1:21 "And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The "great whales" (Hebrew tannin, sea monsters) — the largest creatures ever to live — are created in a single day. Again everything reproduces "after his kind."

Meaning: God makes the enormous and the microscopic with the same word. The blue whale — over thirty metres long, heart the size of a car — and the invisible plankton it eats were both spoken into being on day five. God is not intimidated by size, and He is not too busy for smallness. Bring Him your giant problems and your tiny details; He made both ends of the scale. Job 41 describes the leviathan as a creature only God can handle — and Job needed to see that. When your troubles look like sea monsters, remember Who made the sea and everything in it, and commands it still (Mark 4:39).

GENESIS 1:22 "And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: This is the first blessing spoken in the Bible — and it is spoken over animals. God blesses the fish and birds with fruitfulness.

Meaning: God's first recorded words to living things are a blessing, not a command of toil. Blessing means empowered increase: God doesn't just tell creatures to multiply, He gives them the capacity to do it. The principle stands for you: whatever God commands, He blesses you to do. When He later says to humanity "be fruitful and multiply" (verse 28), He is not merely giving an instruction — He is conferring a grace. Fruitfulness is a blessing before it is a duty. Jesus said, "I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit" (John 15:16). You are a blessed creature in a blessed creation, and the blessing of the beginning still runs through the world God made.

GENESIS 1:23 "And the evening and the morning were the fifth day." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Day five ends. The seas and skies are filled; only the land animals and humanity remain.

Meaning: The waters obeyed the word and the sky obeyed the word, and again the day closes with evening before morning. By now a rhythm is visible: God speaks, it happens, God sees, God blesses, the day ends. This rhythm is the peace of the believer. Because your days were designed by the same mouth that made the seas, you can entrust tomorrow to the God of the fifth day. The psalmist rests in this: "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psalm 4:8). Every evening you close is a testimony that God carried the day — and every morning is an invitation to watch Him carry the next.

GENESIS 1:24 "And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Day six begins. The land now receives its creatures: cattle (domestic animals), creeping things (insects, reptiles), and beasts (wild animals) — each reproducing after its kind.

Meaning: The earth that stood empty (verse 2) is now full. God's timing is perfect: the environment is ready, the food supply is established, and only then are the animals released. God never births before He prepares. Perhaps your promise feels slow — but God is not delaying; He is preparing the ground so what He births will survive. Also see the variety: cattle, creepers, and wild beasts. God is gloriously diverse in creation — no two animals alike, millions of species — yet every kind belongs. The church should reflect this same creativity: many members, one body (1 Corinthians 12:12). God delights in difference; He only demands that each kind reproduce its own kind.

GENESIS 1:25 "And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Before humanity appears, God completes the animal kingdom and pronounces it good. Man arrives into a finished, furnished world.

Meaning: Everything in creation is pronounced "good" — the stage is set, and the crown is about to arrive. This order is the heartbeat of grace: God prepares before He places. Adam did nothing to earn the garden; he woke up inside a finished work and was given it as a gift (Genesis 2:8, 2:15). This is a picture of salvation: "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 2:10). You did not build your redemption; you were born into it by new birth. Enter each day like Adam entered Eden — not as the maker of your blessings, but as the recipient of a good God's finished preparation, commissioned to tend what grace handed you.

GENESIS 1:26 "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The climax of creation. Everything before this was made by simple command — but for humanity God pauses, deliberates, and says "Let US make." The plural "us" hints at the Trinity — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — involved in the making of man.

Meaning: You are not an animal that evolved upward; you are a creature made in the image of God — imago Dei. An image reflects. Within every human being is a mirror designed to show what God is like: rational, moral, creative, relational, immortal. This is why human life has infinite worth — every person, from the unborn to the elderly, carries the divine image. Dominion follows image: because you carry God's likeness, God shares His authority. Man was made to rule the earth as God's representative — a manager under the Owner. Sin marred the mirror, but in Christ the image is being restored: "put on the new man, which is renewed... after the image of him that created him" (Colossians 3:10). You were made to look like Him and to act like Him on the earth.

GENESIS 1:27 "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Note the change of verb: God "created" (bara) — the same word as verse 1. Only here, in all of chapter 1, does God create something in His own image. Humanity is a fresh act of creation, not a continuation.

Meaning: Three truths thunder from this verse. First, every human is created — no one is an accident; your existence is an intentional act of God. Second, both male and female equally carry the image: men and women are equal in dignity and value, different in design and role — together reflecting the full image of God. Third, marriage and gender are part of creation's architecture, not culture's invention; what God created "them" to be cannot be redefined by man. When you feel worthless, remember you are the only creature in the universe stamped with God's own portrait. The devil works hard to mar that image; God worked harder to restore it in Christ — "the express image of his person" (Hebrews 1:3).

GENESIS 1:28 "And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: God blesses humanity and gives the first command ever given to a human being: fruitfulness, multiplication, filling the earth, subduing it, and dominion.

Meaning: This is called the Cultural Mandate — the original job description of humanity. God's blessing carries responsibility: be fruitful (productive), multiply (generational), replenish (develop and cultivate), subdue (bring order out of wildness), have dominion (steward under God). Notice the God-given dignity of work: before sin, before sweat, man was a worker and a ruler. Your career, your farm, your business, your home — all of it is part of "subduing" the earth, which is holy work when done for God's glory. And the blessing came before the command — grace before task, gift before duty. God never sends you on assignment without first blessing you for it.

GENESIS 1:29 "And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: Before man has asked for anything, God has already provided his food. This is the first "Behold" of Scripture — God calling attention to His generosity.

Meaning: "Behold" means look at this — God delights to show what He has given. Man's original diet was plants: grains, herbs, and fruits, given freely, a world without death where nothing had to die for man to eat. God provided before man had needs — provision preceded petition. The same God who at sundry times and in divers manners has already made provision for your salvation before you knew to ask: "my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:19). When you pray for daily bread, you are not begging a stingy god; you are receiving from the hand that stocked a whole planet with food before the first mouth opened.

GENESIS 1:30 "And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: God's provision extends beyond humanity to every animal — the whole food chain is established. "Wherein there is life" — literally, "wherein is a living soul" (nephesh).

Meaning: God cares for all His creatures. "The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season" (Psalm 145:15). Jesus said not one sparrow falls without your Father (Matthew 10:29), and the ravens neither sow nor reap yet God feeds them (Luke 12:24). If God runs a universe where even the creeping things have a menu, will He forget you, who are made in His image? Also note: originally, no creature ate another. Death entered creation through sin (Romans 5:12); peace between man, beast, and food is the mark of Eden, and Isaiah 11:6–9 promises the return of that harmony in the age to come. Creation began vegetarian; creation will end peaceful.

GENESIS 1:31 "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day." ▾ Tap to see the context and meaning
Read in NKJV ↗

Context: The final evaluation of creation. Six times God said "good"; now, with everything complete, He says "very good." On day seven He will rest.

Meaning: Note the progression: individual acts were "good"; the completed work is "very good." God's works are only fully seen as excellent when seen as a whole. Your life is the same — some days look merely good, some look like chaos, but God is producing a completed work (Philippians 1:6), and on the last day the whole will be "very good." Notice too what makes creation very good: it was exactly as God designed, in harmony with its Maker, untainted by sin. The first chapter of the Bible ends in perfection — and the last chapters of the Bible end in perfection too (Revelation 21–22). Everything in between is the story of God bringing His fallen creation back to "very good" through Christ. You are part of that story.

Chapter 1 in One Sentence: God created everything by His word, in wisdom and order, blessing what He made — and humanity, made in His image, is the crown of His creation.

Next installment: Genesis Chapter 2 — the Garden of Eden, the making of woman, and the first marriage.
